evals.name: writeup-from-raw-results
evals.prompt: I've got simulation results sitting in results.csv (columns: rep, dgp, estimator, est, se). Three estimators (gcomp, aipw, tmle), three DGPs (simple, moderate, complex), n=500, 1000 reps, true ATE is 1.0 for all three DGPs. Write me the simulation section for the paper.
evals.expected_output: Organized claim-by-claim, not table-by-table. Each piece of evidence sandwiched: goal stated, evidence shown, interpretation given. Captions name the claim they serve. Design choices get reasons. Should ask what the paper is actually claiming rather than dumping a table.
assertions: Section is organized around claims (claims appear as headings or lead sentences that each piece of evidence then serves), rather than ordered by table number with purpose explained only at the end
Each table or figure is both introduced by a statement of what it will show AND followed by an interpretation tying it back to a claim (the tell-em sandwich)
At least one table or figure caption states the claim it supports, not merely its contents
Design choices are given explicit reasons in the text (why these DGPs, why this estimand, why these performance measures)
Reports the correct qualitative findings from the data: gcomp is badly biased with severe undercoverage in the complex DGP, aipw undercovers moderately in complex, tmle performs best overall
Does not open the results with Monte Carlo SE machinery or a failure/non-convergence count as the headline item
States explicitly what it is assuming the paper claims, since the user never said

evals.name: design-backwards-not-code-first
evals.prompt: I'm writing a paper on a new doubly-robust estimator for the ATE under outcome-dependent sampling. I need to set up the simulation study. Can you help me get started?
evals.expected_output: Starts with the claims the paper makes, sharpens them into answerable goals, mocks up tables/figures BEFORE proposing DGPs or writing code. Should not jump straight to DGP equations or an R script.
assertions: Establishes or asks about the paper's claims before proposing any data-generating process
Sharpens vague goals by naming what is unpinned (at least two of: performance measure, sample size, which DGPs, learners/nuisances, baseline)
Mocks up at least one table or figure (empty cells, or described axes and facets) before specifying DGPs
Does not deliver executable simulation code as the primary or first deliverable
Proposed DGPs are each tied to a stated claim rather than offered as generically reasonable
Mentions DGP diagnostics (overlap/positivity, variance explained or signal-to-noise, or degree of nonlinearity) as things to check
Recommends ramping up repetitions (a tiny run first, then a moderate one) rather than committing to a fixed large number up front

evals.name: results-contradict-claim
evals.prompt: Bad news. My simulation shows the plug-in estimator actually beats my proposed debiased estimator on MSE in the moderate-confounding DGP. Debiasing cuts the bias but the variance blows up. I was going to claim my method dominates. How do I present this?
evals.expected_output: Does not bury or drop the DGP. Walks: check for a bug, understand why theoretically, then narrow the claim with an added condition, framed as a better claim.
assertions: Does not suggest dropping, hiding, or relegating the inconvenient DGP or result
Recommends checking for a bug or implementation error before reinterpreting
Recommends understanding theoretically why the bias-variance tradeoff goes this way
Proposes a concrete rewritten claim with an added scoping condition, in actual sentence form
Frames the narrowed claim as a better claim rather than as a concession
Recommends reporting the unfavorable result with the same prominence as favorable ones

evals.name: code-shared-rerunnable-cached
evals.prompt: Claims and mockups for my simulation are settled. Table 1 compares three learner libraries (main-terms GLM; GLM + MARS; GLM + MARS + random forest, combined by super learner) on RMSE for the outcome regression and the propensity score. Table 2 shows bias, SE and coverage of AIPW and TMLE built on the second and third libraries. Three DGPs, n in {250, 1000}, eventually 1000 reps. Write the R simulation code.
evals.expected_output: One pipeline whose stored learner fits feed both tables; a run function that takes subsets of every factor; seeds derived from each dataset's name; each dataset made of training, validation and estimation draws of the same size, with the super learner choosing on the validation draw; per-learner predictions on the validation and estimation draws cached in a gitignored directory with keys that cover data and code; a small run and a pilot with the same code before the full run.
assertions: Both tables are computed from one set of datasets and one set of learner fits; the estimator code reads stored predictions and does not refit learners in a separate script
The run entry point accepts subsets of DGPs, sample sizes, repetitions, libraries and estimators, so any one of them can be rerun alone
Each dataset's seed is derived from its DGP, sample size and repetition, not from loop position or a single per-repetition seed shared across DGPs

Each dataset is three independent draws of the same size n (training, validation, estimation): learners are fit on the first, the super learner chooses or weights them on the second, and the estimators run on the third, with no cross-fitting or inner cross-validation
Base-learner predictions are cached to local disk, including the validation-draw predictions the super learner needs, so a library is assembled from stored predictions without refitting
The cache directory is gitignored, or the response says to add it to .gitignore before the first run
Cache keys cover the inputs and the code or specification that produced each entry, so a changed learner, DGP or seed cannot return a stale entry
Recommends a tiny run and then a pilot of roughly 100 to 200 repetitions, with the same code, before the full 1000-repetition run
